summary.text: Electrochemistry is the branch of physical chemistry that links electrical potential difference to identifiable chemical change.
In electrochemical reactions such as electrolysis, batteries and fuel cells, electrons travel through an electric circuit instead of passing directly between atoms, ions or molecules.
The field's birth is credited to Luigi Galvani in the late 18th century, and Alessandro Volta then developed the first practical battery.

items.prompt: In a battery, how do electrons get from one reaction site to the other?

options.label: Through an electric circuit, not directly between atoms or molecules
By hopping straight from molecule to molecule in the liquid
By dissolving in the electrolyte until they reach the end
By turning into ions that then flow back

items.explain: In electrochemical reactions, electrons are not transferred directly between atoms, ions or molecules but via the electric circuit. That distinguishes them from conventional chemical reactions.

items.prompt: One device uses electricity to drive a chemical change, as in splitting water. Another makes electricity from a chemical reaction. Which is electrochemical?

options.label: Only the first
Both of them
Only the second
Neither, since they belong to physics

items.explain: A reaction driven by an electrical potential difference, as in electrolysis, and one that produces a potential difference, as in a battery or fuel cell, are both electrochemical reactions.

items.prompt: Volta rejected Galvani's idea of 'animal electricity'. What did his experiments still produce?

options.label: The first electric generator
The first fuel cell
The first practical battery
Two laws of electrochemistry

items.explain: Volta's experimentation led him to develop the first practical battery, even though he rejected the 'animal electric fluid'. The generator, fuel cell and laws came from others.

items.prompt: Early cells suffered from polarization. How did John Daniell's cell get rid of the hydrogen gas at the positive electrode?

options.label: By adding more zinc to the liquid
By sealing the cell so the gas could not escape
By enlarging the positive electrode
By introducing copper ions into the solution near that electrode

items.explain: Daniell's cell solved the polarization problem by introducing copper ions near the positive electrode, which eliminated hydrogen gas generation.

items.prompt: A salt dissolves in water. What did Arrhenius conclude in his thesis about such electrolytes?

options.label: They stay whole and carry current as intact molecules
They split to varying degrees into positive and negative ions
They split into neutral atoms of the same charge
They turn into ice-like crystals around each ion

items.explain: Arrhenius concluded that electrolytes dissolved in water become, to varying degrees, split or dissociated into electrically opposite positive and negative ions.

items.prompt: Hall and Héroult found an efficient way to make aluminium. What did they pass electricity through?

options.label: Molten alumina
Liquid ammonia
Dilute sulfuric acid
Pure water

items.explain: The Hall–Héroult process obtains aluminium by electrolysis of molten alumina.

paragraphs.heading: What it studies
paragraphs.text: Electrochemistry is the part of physical chemistry that connects electrical potential difference with chemical change you can identify. In its reactions, electrons move between electrodes through a conductor, usually an outside electric circuit, though not always, as electroless plating shows. The electrodes are separated by an electrolyte, which conducts ions but does not conduct electrons. The study of electrochemistry at the nanoscale is called nanoelectrochemistry.

paragraphs.heading: What makes a reaction electrochemical
paragraphs.text: A reaction counts as electrochemical when a potential difference drives it, as in electrolysis, or when the reaction itself creates a potential difference, as in a battery or a fuel cell. In other chemical reactions, electrons pass directly between atoms, ions or molecules. In electrochemical ones they travel through the circuit instead. That difference is what sets an electrochemical reaction apart from a conventional one.

paragraphs.heading: Early sparks
paragraphs.text: People began to understand electrical matters in the 1500s, when the English scientist William Gilbert spent 17 years experimenting mostly with magnetism and partly with electricity. In 1663 Otto von Guericke built the first electric generator. It was a sulfur ball inside a glass globe, turned by a crank, and it gave off a spark when a pad was rubbed against it. By the mid-1700s Charles François de Cisternay du Fay had found two kinds of static electricity, and that like charges repel while unlike charges attract.

paragraphs.heading: Frogs and the first battery
paragraphs.text: The Italian physician and anatomist Luigi Galvani is credited with the birth of electrochemistry. In a 1791 essay he connected chemical reactions with electricity, arguing that animal tissue held its own animal electricity that activated nerves and muscles touched by metal probes. Alessandro Volta rejected this, saying the frog's legs were responding to differences between the metals. Volta's experiments led him to the first practical battery, which used zinc and delivered current much longer than any other device then known.

paragraphs.heading: Splitting water and isolating metals
paragraphs.text: In 1800 William Nicholson and Johann Wilhelm Ritter used Volta's battery to break water into hydrogen and oxygen, a process called electrolysis. Ritter soon went on to discover electroplating. Humphry Davy's electrolysis work convinced him that simple cells make electricity through chemical action. That work led directly, in 1808, to metallic sodium and potassium being isolated by electrolysis of their molten salts.

paragraphs.heading: Laws and practical cells
paragraphs.text: Michael Faraday's experiments brought him, in 1832, to his two laws of electrochemistry. In 1836 John Daniell invented a cell that solved a problem called polarization: he put copper ions in the solution near the positive electrode, so no hydrogen gas formed there. William Grove built the first fuel cell in 1839. In 1868 Georges Leclanché patented a cell that became the forerunner of the zinc–carbon cell, the world's first widely used battery.

paragraphs.heading: Ions and aluminium
paragraphs.text: In his 1884 thesis, Svante Arrhenius concluded that electrolytes dissolved in water split, to differing degrees, into positive and negative ions. Two years later, in 1886, Paul Héroult and Charles M. Hall developed an efficient way to obtain aluminium by electrolysis of molten alumina. It is now known as the Hall–Héroult process.
